doc.title: Al Gallodoro interviewed by Monk Rowe, Oneonta, New York, December 28, 2005

title: Touring units, 'The Hour of Parting' and conductor Erno Rappe
summary: Idle time during units, a 1928 tune, Erno Rappe and the Center Theater ice show, and his son's flat Selmer saxophone.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Reeds, mouthpieces and horns: the reed player's gear

blocks.x: Yeah. Then on occasion they had a unit, like the California Collegiates, and all we played was the overture and for 45 minutes we did nothing. We went downstairs and played poker or whatever, and we’d come back. And I’ll never forget this. The famous tune that they came out with, and JoAnn my accompanist knows and we play it on occasion, was “The Hour of Parting.” It was written in 1928. “The Hour of Parting.” And the famous conductor at the music hall — now see how my mind skips me now — the famous conductor, he was great. He opened the music hall. Erno Rappe. Erno Rappe. Now today that means nothing to anyone. He was a great musician, great conductor. And when I went into the Center Theater Ice Show “It Happens on Ice,” he opened the show as a conductor. Then he handed it to David Mendoza, who was the real conductor. But he
broke the show in, Erno Rappe. Yeah. And his son was a pretty good saxophone player. Can I tell you something about his son?

He played Selmer also. And I said, “Bob,” I says, “you play nice, you get a good sound, but man your high notes are so flat.” And this went on night after night. I said, “Let me try your horn.” I apologized. I said, “It’s not you, Bob, it’s the horn.” They were flat. They were known to be flat, some of the old cigar cutter. They were known to be flat. Then they made them, not in tune but they made them sharp. They didn’t go right there to pitch you know. I spoke to Marcel Mule about that. He says I know they’re sharp but better that way because it’s easier to come down, and that’s the truth.
